collective unconscious.title: Collective Unconscious
collective unconscious.definition: A part of the unconscious mind shared by all humanity, containing inherited archetypes and universal symbols that transcend individual experience.
collective unconscious.example: The recurring appearance of flood myths across unrelated cultures suggests a shared psychic heritage — a collective unconscious from which these stories emerge independently.

individuation.title: Individuation
individuation.definition: The lifelong process of integrating the conscious and unconscious aspects of the psyche to become a whole, undivided Self — distinct from mere ego development.
individuation.example: A person who begins to acknowledge their shadow qualities rather than projecting them onto others is taking a crucial step in individuation.

archetype.title: Archetype
archetype.definition: A universal, inherited pattern of thought or symbolic image derived from the collective unconscious. Archetypes are not images themselves but tendencies to form certain images.
archetype.example: The 'Wise Old Man' who appears as a guide in dreams — whether as Gandalf, Dumbledore, or an unnamed sage — is an archetypal figure.

shadow.title: Shadow
shadow.definition: The unconscious aspect of the personality that the conscious ego does not identify with — often containing repressed weaknesses, desires, and instincts, but also hidden strengths.
shadow.example: Someone who prides themselves on patience may have a shadow that contains intense rage, which occasionally erupts in dreams or unexpected outbursts.

anima.title: Anima
anima.definition: The unconscious feminine side of a man's personality, serving as a bridge to the deeper layers of the unconscious. It often appears in dreams as a mysterious female figure.
anima.example: A man who dreams repeatedly of an unknown woman leading him into a forest is encountering his anima, which is inviting him to explore his unconscious.

animus.title: Animus
animus.definition: The unconscious masculine side of a woman's personality, often manifesting as inner convictions, opinions, or dream figures that carry authority.
animus.example: A woman who dreams of a panel of judges or a powerful male figure giving pronouncements may be encountering her animus.

synchronicity.title: Synchronicity
synchronicity.definition: A meaningful coincidence of outer and inner events that are not causally connected. Jung proposed this as an acausal connecting principle alongside causality.
synchronicity.example: Thinking intensely about a deceased friend and then immediately receiving a letter they had written before dying — the timing is meaningful but not causal.

persona.title: Persona
persona.definition: The social mask or face we present to the world — a compromise between the individual and society's expectations. From the Latin word for 'mask' worn by actors.
persona.example: The professional demeanor a therapist adopts during sessions is persona — necessary and useful, but potentially dangerous if mistaken for the true self.

active imagination.title: Active Imagination
active imagination.definition: A meditation technique developed by Jung in which the contents of the unconscious are translated into images, narratives, or personified figures, and then consciously engaged with.
active imagination.example: Sitting quietly and allowing a dream figure to 'speak,' then responding to it in writing — not controlling the fantasy but participating in it.

mandala.title: Mandala
mandala.definition: A circular symbolic form representing the totality of the Self. Jung found that patients spontaneously drew mandalas during critical phases of individuation.
mandala.example: A patient who begins spontaneously drawing circles with four quadrants during a period of inner turmoil is unconsciously creating a mandala — an attempt at psychic self-healing.

projection.title: Projection
projection.definition: An unconscious process whereby a personal quality — whether positive or negative — is perceived as belonging to another person or the external world rather than to oneself.
projection.example: Intensely disliking someone for being 'arrogant' when the quality you're reacting to is actually your own unacknowledged arrogance — that's shadow projection.

complex.title: Complex
complex.definition: A cluster of emotionally charged associations in the unconscious, organized around a central archetype, that can temporarily take over the ego and drive behavior.
complex.example: A 'mother complex' might cause someone to unconsciously seek nurturing in every relationship, or to rebel against any perceived authority figure.

libido.title: Libido (Jungian)
libido.definition: In Jung's broader definition, libido is general psychic energy — not merely sexual energy as Freud defined it. It is the energy that drives all psychological activity.
libido.example: When someone becomes deeply absorbed in painting or spiritual practice, Jung would say their libido has been channeled into creative or transcendent expression.

transcendent function.title: Transcendent Function
transcendent function.definition: The psychic function that mediates between opposites — conscious and unconscious, thinking and feeling — producing a new, third position that transcends both.
transcendent function.example: A conflict between duty and desire that resolves not by choosing one side but by discovering a creative solution that honors both — that's the transcendent function at work.

enantiodromia.title: Enantiodromia
enantiodromia.definition: The tendency of things to turn into their opposites, especially when taken to an extreme. A principle Jung borrowed from Heraclitus and applied to psychic processes.
enantiodromia.example: A culture that becomes excessively rational and suppresses emotion will eventually erupt in irrational mass movements — the repressed opposite returns with force.
